description: Starter beta! Voice Library. AI may select from these records but may not invent quotations.

voices.name: Moses
voices.era_note: Traditional biblical chronology; exact historical dating is debated.
voices.source_basis: The Torah / Pentateuch, especially speeches attributed to Moses in Deuteronomy.

quotes.text: Choose life, then, that you and your descendants may live.
quotes.context: Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses places a real choice before Israel: life and good, or death and evil. The line is about choosing a direction and living into it.

voices.name: Socrates
voices.era_note: Socrates left no writings; his voice is preserved principally through Plato and Xenophon.
voices.source_basis: Plato's dialogues, especially the Apology, with Socrates' words transmitted by Plato.

quotes.text: The unexamined life is not worth living.
quotes.context: In Plato's account of his defense at trial, Socrates argues that examining ourselves and our beliefs is part of a life worth living.

voices.name: Jesus
voices.era_note: Approximate setting of Jesus' public ministry.

quotes.text: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest.
quotes.context: Jesus addresses people carrying burdens and offers rest rather than pretending the burden is not real.

quotes.text: For when I am weak, then I am strong.
quotes.context: Paul writes about a persistent weakness he wanted removed and the paradox of discovering strength in the place he felt weak.

voices.name: Polycarp
voices.era_note: Approximate period commonly associated with his Letter to the Philippians.
voices.source_basis: Polycarp's surviving Letter to the Philippians.

quotes.text: When you can do good, defer it not.
quotes.context: Polycarp urges ordinary Christians to stay firm, care for one another, and not postpone the good they are able to do.

voices.name: Augustine
voices.era_note: Approximate beginning of the composition of Confessions.
voices.source_basis: Augustine's Confessions and other surviving works.

quotes.text: You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in You.
quotes.context: Augustine opens Confessions by naming a restlessness at the center of human desire and directing it toward God.

voices.name: Benedict
voices.era_note: Approximate period traditionally associated with the Rule of Saint Benedict.

quotes.text: Listen carefully, my son, to the master's instructions, and attend to them with the ear of your heart.
quotes.context: The Rule begins not with a command to achieve more, but with an invitation to listen deeply and pay attention.

voices.name: Thomas Aquinas
voices.era_note: Approximate beginning of the Summa Theologiae.
voices.source_basis: Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae and related surviving works.

quotes.text: Nothing satisfies man's natural desire, except the perfect good which is Happiness.
quotes.location: I-II, Question 5, Article 8, Reply to Objection 3
quotes.context: Aquinas distinguishes getting things we happen to want from the deeper human desire for a good capable of truly satisfying us.

voices.name: Catherine of Siena
voices.era_note: Her surviving letters span years of intense Church and political conflict.
voices.source_basis: Catherine of Siena's surviving letters and Dialogue.

quotes.text: The love which I bear to you makes me speak with boldness.
quotes.context: Writing during a Church crisis, Catherine explains that love—not hostility—is what drives her to speak plainly and boldly.

voices.name: Martin Luther
voices.source_basis: Luther's surviving writings and contemporary records of the Diet of Worms.

quotes.text: My conscience is captive to the Word of God.
quotes.context: Pressed to retract his writings, Luther framed his refusal around Scripture, reason, and conscience.

voices.name: John Henry Newman
voices.era_note: Publication year of An Essay in Aid of a Grammar of Assent.
voices.source_basis: Newman's Apologia Pro Vita Sua, Grammar of Assent, and related writings.

quotes.text: To fear argument is to doubt the conclusion.
quotes.work: An Essay in Aid of a Grammar of Assent
quotes.context: Newman argues that honest examination need not be the enemy of conviction; fear of examination can itself reveal uncertainty.

voices.name: C.S. Lewis
voices.era_note: Publication year of A Grief Observed.
voices.source_basis: C.S. Lewis's published books, essays, and letters. Modern copyrighted material is represented only by brief sourced excerpts.

quotes.text: No one ever told me that grief felt so like fear.
quotes.context: Lewis wrote A Grief Observed after the death of his wife, Joy Davidman, recording grief as he actually experienced it rather than smoothing it into a tidy answer.
